text.p: A proposal for legislation to deregulate Pennsylvania's electric power industry was made public Wednesday.
It was quickly endorsed by PP&L Resources Inc's Pennsylvania Power & Light Co subsidiary as representing "a shared vision of a new electricity business in Pennsylvania."

Gov. Tom Ridge is expected to seek legislative approval of the proposal before the end of November, PP&L spokesman Jim Marsh said. It was produced by a panel Ridge created last month that includes regulators along with representatives of utilities and power users, as well as consumer advocates.
The bill, because of the way it was crafted, is representative of the needs of all those who have a stake in the state's electricity business, PP&L chief executive Wiliam Hecht said.
Other utilities operating in Pennsylvania include units of GPU Inc, PECO Energy Co, DQE Inc, Ohio Edison Co, Orange and Rockland Utilities Inc, UGI Corp and Allegheny Power System Inc.
"All major interests were represented as this legislative proposal was being written," he said.
"The result is a proposal that will protect the interests of all those involved as we move toward a more competitive electricity marketplace."

"This legislation, if enacted swiftly, would provide Pennsylvania with a significant economic development advantage in this region of the country. A competitive electricity marketplace sends a strong message that Pennsylvania supports economic development," said Hecht.
A summary of the proposal released on a Public Utilities Commission hearing said electric distribution companies will continue to be the supplier of last resort.
It said this is to ensure the availability of universal electric service and said the commission will ensure that adequate generation reserves exist to maintain reliable electric service.
The commission would license all power suppliers to ensure financial responsibility and develop standards for power generators, power brokers, marketers and aggregators.
The proposal calls for all transmission and distribution rates to be capped for at least four and a half years and possibly as long as nine years.
It would also cap generation rates for up to nine years.

Together, Marsh explained, the two caps mean that customers who choose to do nothing as choice becomes available would see no increase in rates over those in effect at the beginning of 1997 if the proposal is adopted.
This is a ceiling on what the utility can charge, he noted, not a floor. Competition could well force the actual rates down from the capped level.

The proposal calls for retail choice to be phased in over the next four years with 33 percent of all customer load allowed to choose a power supplier at the end of 1998, 66 percent by the end of 1999 and 100 percent by the end of 2000.

The commission can order utilities to conduct pilot programs beginnin April 1, 1997, under the proposal. Five percent of a utility's peak load would be committted to a pilot program running at least one year.
The proposal calls for recovery of stranded costs and transition costs by issuing transition bonds and says savings associated with this financing will be used to provide rate reductions.
It says cooperatives and municipal systems may participate in retail competition but are not subject to the law unless they elect to provide service outside their territory.
The summary also says "state tax revenue paid by utilities will remain at a level to ensure tax neutrality in order to protect the state's general fund from any revenue loss.
It would give the commission power to consider the impact of mergers and acquisitions on the retail market.
A member of the group making this proposal, Public Utility Commissioner John Hanger, pointed out during the deliberations that "this isn't the deregulation of the electric industry."
Pointing out that "regulation will remain," he said electric power generation and distribution will still be "one of the most heavily regulated (industries)."
